items.title: Panama Francis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995
items.q: I joined Roy Eldridge... he asked me if I would like to join his band... I’m there setting my drums up... Roy said 'I don’t know where he is.' So he said 'well who is that setting up the drums there?' ... 'oh, that’s Panama'

ctx.x: Do different musicians that play different ways ‘cause you to react certain ways as a drummer?

Well yes. I am very competitive. In fact when I worked with Roy Eldridge, he was of the same mentality. And we used to go out and look for jam sessions and look for guys to cut you know. Because back then it was just like sports. I mean music was like sports. You and I can be the best of friends. And you play drums, I play drums. But when we got on the bandstand it was a different ball game. Everything went out the window. I mean I’m competing with you and you are competing with me. And that’s why, you know,…
You know tell us about your concept of what the drummer does in the ensemble. What role does the drummer bring to jazz music?

items.title: 61521_David Albert Francis oral history interview
items.q: But I had this job lined up with Roy Eldridge, and so I joined his band... Roy would make me go in the room next door, and get the music book, and learn how to read music

ctx.x: And I asked if I could sit in, and they looked at me, because at that time, I only weighed 121 lbs; I was the littlest guy, and I looked like I was about 14 years old.

So they asked me how old I was, so I told them I was 18, but I said I'd be 19 in December --and this was August. So they said, "And you can play?" -- and I said, "I think so." So I got up on the bandstand and I started playing, and everybody started looking around at me, and I played the same thing when I went to Jocks and the same at the Rennie.
